title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
hook: which comes first in a morning, a thought or a want? the hymn's fourth verse gives its answer
carry: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta's third verse: darkness hidden by darkness, until the One was born by the power of heat. What warmed something blank into starting? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.

Which comes first in a morning, a thought or a want? Watch the first minute after an alarm sometime. Before a plan, before a sentence forms, there is often a lean. Toward the warm blanket. Toward coffee. Toward the phone on the nightstand. Only after the lean does the mind start talking, building reasons, making a list. The Nasadiya Sukta asks the same question on the largest scale there is. The One has just been born out of the dark. What happens next? The fourth verse answers, and its answer is not a thought.
screen: `A THOUGHT OR A WANT?` → `FIRST, A LEAN.` → `THEN THE MIND STARTS TALKING.`

segments.voice: The verse opens with kama. Desire came upon it in the beginning, it says, desire that was the first seed of mind. Kama is the ordinary Sanskrit word for desire, wanting, love. It's also the name of one of the aims of a human life in Hindu teaching: pleasure and love. And here it stands at the very start, before mind. Not desire as a problem to be fixed. Desire as a seed. First the wanting, then the mind that grows out of it. Then the verse turns from the cosmos to people. The poets, it says, the kavis, searched in their hearts with wisdom, and found the bond of what is in what is not. The word for bond is bandhu. It also means kin, a relative, the people you're tied to. So the poets found that being has a kinship with non-being, a family tie running back into the dark. Notice where they looked. Not up at the sky. Not into a record of what happened. In the heart. The hymn doesn't claim they saw the beginning. It says they searched inward and found a connection there. That's a quiet claim about how this kind of knowing works: you can't go back and watch the start, but you can look into your own heart and find what ties you to it. This week began with what the Rig Veda is, a collection of hymns, and then settled into this one. Its verses so far have moved from neither being nor non-being, to darkness on darkness, to heat, and now to desire, and to poets looking inward for the bond.
screen: `KAMA: DESIRE, THE FIRST SEED OF MIND.` · `THE POETS SEARCHED IN THEIR HEARTS.` · `BANDHU: A BOND, A KINSHIP.` · `WHAT IS, TIED TO WHAT IS NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for the lean underneath. Settle, and let the breath run on its own. Wait for the next thought to arrive. When it does, don't follow it. Instead, look just underneath it, for the want that came first. A wish to be comfortable. A wish to be finished. A wish to be loved. Don't judge the want, and don't feed it. Just notice it, the way the poets searched their hearts, and come back to the breath. Then wait for the next one. If you pray, you can offer each want as you find it. The bell holds the time.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. In its fourth verse, desire is the first seed of mind, and the poets find the bond of what is in what is not. Today's word.

Your line: the Nasadiya Sukta, the hymn of creation, who really knows? Today, once, before you act on a plan, look for the want underneath it. A week on the hill, done. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.

original.note: Sanskrit: desire, wanting, love. In Rig Veda 10.129.4 it is the first seed of mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: in Hindu texts, desire is only a problem to get rid of.
what it means: in this hymn desire stands at the start, the first seed from which mind grows.
what a scholar hears: sato bandhum asati nir avindan, 'they found the bond of the existent in the non-existent,' with bandhu, the word for kin, as the link.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.129.4 (desire came upon it in the beginning, the first seed of mind; the poets, searching in their hearts with wisdom, found the bond of being in non-being)

notes: Week end (1247–1253): the look-back names the week's arc from the index (what the Rig Veda is, then the Nasadiya Sukta) and recaps verses 1–3 as covered on 1250–1252.

Sanskrit of 10.129.4 (kāmas tad agre sam avartatādhi manaso retaḥ prathamaṃ yad āsīt; sato bandhum asati nir avindan hṛdi pratīṣyā kavayo manīṣā) given from memory in simplified transliteration; confirm.
'Retas' (seed) is given as 'seed' throughout; the word can also mean semen. Kept as 'seed'.
Kama linked to the purushartha 'one of the aims of a human life'; confirm the gloss 'the enjoyment of what's good'.
Bandhu glossed as bond / kin; confirm. The trapdoor's 'the word for kin' is a gloss, not an etymology.
'There is often a lean' before thought in the hook is an observation offered as a question, not a claim about the listener.
Editor: kama's purushartha gloss reworded ('pleasure and love') and the generalization 'Hindus use' removed; otherwise unchanged.
